issues.explanation: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events are not well linked to the stated trauma of witnessing childhood domestic violence, especially when the other trigger items center on male presence and shouting. This trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

Listening for signs that someone is entering the home suggests a burglary/home-intrusion threat theme, which is weakly connected to the selected trauma-specific cues and memory/appraisal content centered on domestic violence. It pulls the threat profile toward external break-in danger rather than reenacted interpersonal violence.

Noticing weapons or dangerous objects in any environment implies a generalized weapon-attack threat theme, but the trauma type and the rest of the items do not support a weapon-focused formulation. This makes the threat node less coherent with the memory and appraisal content.

'I have failed in my most important role in life' is a broad role-failure appraisal that is not clearly anchored to the selected trauma memories or other appraisals. The other negative appraisals emphasize weakness and disconnection; this item introduces a different theme without enough support elsewhere in the profile.

Drug use is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The strongest formulation link is Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, and the other strategies clearly fit trigger-driven internal threat management, whereas drug use introduces a more severe coping pattern without corresponding support from the other selected items.

vignette:
Carlos is a 64-year-old jeweler, divorced for over a decade, who sought treatment for what he described as a lifetime of “waiting for the other shoe to drop.” He grew up in a small apartment in San Antonio, where his father’s violent rages were a fixture of his early years. He still sees those nights in snapshot images: the flash of a ceramic lamp shattering against the wall, the silver glint of a letter opener his father once snatched from the kitchen drawer, his mother’s voice rising until it cracked. Each memory is vivid and detailed, as if frozen in amber, and when it surfaces he is flooded with guilt—guilt that he did nothing, guilt that he survived unscathed while his mother bore the bruises. These memories are not just painful; they are instructions. Whenever they come, Carlos begins to monitor his own thoughts obsessively, scanning for any hint of the same violent potential he fears lives inside him. He also tries to suppress the images entirely, pushing them down with work or silence, but the effort leaves him drained and more convinced that he is weak. The suppression itself kept his mind on edge, and ordinary moments—a customer walking in, a phone ringing—began to feel like potential flashpoints, turning his daily work into a cascade of triggers he could no longer ignore.

For decades, Carlos managed by staying busy. As a jeweler, he spent long hours alone at his bench, repairing watches and setting stones—work that demanded intense focus and kept his hands occupied. But his daily environment has become a minefield. A customer raising his voice over a repair bill triggers a cascade: Carlos’s eyes flick to the glass cases, then to the small hammer on his bench, calculating whether it could be used as a weapon. He watches every male customer with hypervigilance, reading body language for signs of aggression. Shouting, male presence, and direct confrontations have become unbearable. He has come to believe that if he relaxes—even for a moment—something terrible will happen, so he avoids any quiet pause, filling every second with motion or thought. Because he never stayed still long enough to discover that the danger might not arrive, his body remained locked in a state of high alert, the sense of threat as vivid and urgent as if the event were still happening. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found the world had become dense with reminders he could not stop reading — every raised voice, every quick movement, every male customer stepping through the door now seemed to carry a warning. This constant threat monitoring only reinforces his negative appraisals: he has failed in his most important role as a man and protector, he is weak for being so afraid, and he has lost his connection to the close-knit Latin American community he once valued, because he cannot bear the noise and unpredictability of family gatherings.

The causal cycles are relentless. A memory of his father’s face tightening before a blow will make Carlos glance around his workshop, noticing the metal shears, the small torch, the heavy ring mandrel—all potential weapons. That threat appraisal then sends him back to the memory with fresh guilt, confirming that he is still the frightened boy who could not act. When a confrontation does occur, even a minor disagreement with a colleague, Carlos feels his negative self-beliefs solidify: he should have been stronger, he should have stopped it, he is a failure. These beliefs, in turn, make him more sensitive to any raised voice or male presence, so he starts scanning exits before the argument is over. His maladaptive strategies—suppressing thoughts, monitoring for signs of craziness, refusing to let down his guard—paradoxically make the memories more intrusive, because the effort of suppression keeps the trauma front and center. And every time he suppresses, he reinforces the idea that the memories are too dangerous to face, which deepens his sense of weakness and isolation.

Carlos finally came to therapy because the avoidance is no longer working. A few weeks ago, a new client—a large, loud man—shouted about a repair delay, and Carlos felt his chest tighten so severely that he excused himself and locked himself in the bathroom, trembling. That evening, alone in his apartment, he realized he had not spoken to his sister in three months, had not attended a single family party in over a year, and could no longer trust his own perception of safety. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, but he is also desperate to stop the loop. What he most hopes for is to feel the ground beneath his feet again—to sit quietly in a room with another man and not watch the shadows.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that Carlos's maladaptive strategies (suppression, monitoring, avoidance) lead to an increased perception or occurrence of triggers (external cues).
The vignette does not convey that Carlos's maladaptive strategies cause an increased sense of threat; instead, strategies are responses to threat or reinforce negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that Carlos's maladaptive strategies (suppression, monitoring, avoidance) lead to an increased perception or occurrence of triggers (external cues).
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not convey that Carlos's maladaptive strategies cause an increased sense of threat; instead, strategies are responses to threat or reinforce negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
